Literal Interpretation

The Divine Call to Abraham

Genesis chapter 12 marks a decisive turning point in sacred history. After the account of primeval history culminating in the dispersion of nations at Babel, God now selects one man through whom He will work out His plan of salvation for all peoples. The chapter opens with the Lord's command to Abram: "Go forth out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and out of thy father's house, and come into the land which I shall show thee" (Gen 12:1).

St. Augustine, in his monumental City of God, recognizes the theological significance of this moment:

"God's promises made to Abraham are now to be considered; for in these the oracles of our God, that is, of the true God, began to appear more openly concerning the godly people, whom prophetic authority foretold."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI

The command is threefold: leave your country, your kindred, and your father's house. Each level of separation represents an increasing degree of detachment from natural ties and worldly security. Abram is called to abandon the familiar for the unknown, trusting solely in God's word and promise.

The Threefold Promise

Accompanying the command is a threefold promise (Gen 12:2-3): God will make of Abram a great nation, God will bless him and make his name great, and through him all the families of the earth shall be blessed. Augustine observes that two distinct promises are contained here:

"Two things are promised to Abraham, the one, that his seed should possess the land of Canaan... but the other far more excellent, not about the carnal but the spiritual seed, through which he is the father, not of the one Israelite nation, but of all nations who follow the footprints of his faith."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI

The Chronological Question

A notable difficulty arises from the text. Genesis 11 records Terah's death in Haran at age 205, yet Abram departs at age 75. If Abram was born when Terah was 70, Terah would have been only 145 when Abram left. Augustine addresses this apparent discrepancy:

"When, after the record of the death of Terah, the father of Abraham, we next read, 'And the Lord said to Abram, Get you out of your country...' it is not to be supposed, because this follows in the order of the narrative, that it also followed in the chronological order of events. For if it were so, there would be an insoluble difficulty."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI

Augustine resolves this by explaining that the call came earlier: "God had spoken to Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Haran; but that he came to Haran with his father, keeping in mind the precept of God, and that he went out thence in his own seventy-fifth year, which was his father's 145th." This interpretation is confirmed by St. Stephen's speech in Acts 7:2-4, which places the initial call in Ur of the Chaldees.

The Journey to Canaan

Abram's obedience was immediate and complete. "So Abram went out as the Lord had commanded him" (Gen 12:4). He took with him his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, all their possessions, and the souls they had acquired in Haran. They entered the land of Canaan and traveled to Sichem, to the vale of More, where the Canaanites then dwelt in the land.

St. John Chrysostom, in his Homilies on Genesis, emphasizes Abram's exemplary faith and obedience. His motive for examining the patriarchal narratives was to show "how the just forebears of the Israelites, in a time when both the law and the Gospel were yet unpreached, were able to live Christian lives with only simple trust in God and the balanced, almost ingenuous manners of antiquity."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis

The Theophany and the First Altar

At Sichem, the Lord appeared to Abram and confirmed: "To thy seed will I give this land" (Gen 12:7). In response, Abram built an altar to the Lord. Augustine notes the significance of this promise:

"When God later appeared to Abram and said 'Unto your seed will I give this land,' nothing is promised about that seed in which he is made the father of all nations, but only about that by which he is the father of the one Israelite nation; for by this seed that land was possessed."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI

Abram then moved to a mountain between Bethel and Hai, pitched his tent, and built a second altar, where he invoked the name of the Lord. These altars mark the beginning of true worship in the promised land.

The Descent into Egypt

A famine arose in Canaan, and Abram journeyed southward into Egypt. Fearful that the Egyptians would kill him on account of Sarai's beauty, Abram instructed her to say she was his sister. Indeed, Pharaoh's princes commended Sarai to Pharaoh, and she was taken into his house, while Abram received sheep, oxen, and servants.

The Catholic Encyclopedia summarizes the patristic concern with this episode: "Philo, Theodoret, Procopius of Gaza, Origen, St. John Chrysostom, St. Ambrose and St. Augustine, and many others besides of the Fathers of the Church have done their best to explain this passage plausibly and to render it acceptable." While Sarai was technically his half-sister, the deception troubled many interpreters. The Fathers generally acknowledged the lower moral standards of the patriarchal age while also seeing in the narrative a type of later events.

Catholic Encyclopedia, "Abraham"

Divine Intervention

The Lord afflicted Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai. Discovering the truth, Pharaoh rebuked Abram: "Why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife?" (Gen 12:18). He restored Sarai to Abram and sent them away with all their possessions. The narrative concludes with Abram departing from Egypt, enriched rather than impoverished by the experience.

This episode demonstrates both human weakness and divine faithfulness. Though Abram's faith faltered in the face of famine and fear, God preserved His promise by protecting Sarai and bringing the family safely out of Egypt.

Allegorical Interpretation

Abraham as Type of the Believer

The allegorical sense of Genesis 12 reveals Christ and His Church hidden beneath the historical narrative. The call of Abram from Ur and Haran is a type of the Christian's call from the world to the life of faith. Just as Abram was summoned to leave his country, kindred, and father's house, so every disciple must renounce the world, the flesh, and the devil to follow Christ.

St. Augustine interprets the command spiritually:

"When God says 'Get you out of your country, and from your kindred, and from your father's house,' this means, not that he should cast out his body from thence, for he had already done that, but that he should tear away his soul."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI

The departure from one's country signifies detachment from earthly attachments; from kindred, freedom from carnal relationships that hinder the spiritual life; from father's house, liberation from inherited errors and sins. Christ Himself declared: "If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple" (Lk 14:26).

The Blessing to All Nations: Christ and the Church

The promise that "in thee shall all the kindred of the earth be blessed" (Gen 12:3) is the first clear prophecy of the universal scope of salvation. St. Paul explicitly identifies this promise as the Gospel preached beforehand: "The Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the heathen through faith, declared beforehand unto Abraham, 'In thee shall all nations be blessed'" (Gal 3:8).

St. Irenaeus of Lyon develops this Christological interpretation:

"Abraham was not only the prophet of faith, but also the father of those who from among the Gentiles believe in Jesus Christ, because his faith and ours are one and the same: for he believed in things future, as if they were already accomplished, because of the promise of God."

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book IV

The "seed" of Abraham through whom this blessing comes is Christ Himself. As Irenaeus further explains: "The wages of Christ are human beings, who from various and diverse nations come together into one cohort of faith, as the Father promised Him." The Church, drawn from every nation and tongue, is the fulfillment of the promise to Abram.

Cyril of Alexandria's Typological Method

St. Cyril of Alexandria, in his Glaphyra on the Pentateuch, exemplifies the patristic approach to finding Christ in the patriarchal narratives. His method "begins with a consideration of the historia, where the Alexandrian patriarch deals with the text at the literal level... The exposition then moves on to the theoria, Cyril's preferred term for the contemplation of the spiritual sense—the mystery of Christ which he firmly held lay hidden beneath the surface of the Old Testament text. With great adeptness and consistency Cyril identifies elements within the ancient narratives as figures, or 'types and shadows,' of the Lord Jesus Christ, the Church, and the teachings of the gospel."

Introduction to Cyril of Alexandria, Glaphyra on the Pentateuch

Abraham's Altars and Christian Worship

The altars Abram built at Sichem and Bethel prefigure the worship of the Church. The altar, in patristic understanding, symbolizes "acknowledgement of, approach to, and appreciation of God—in other words, worship." Origen teaches that the altars of the Old Testament all foreshadowed the person and sacrificial work of Christ. When Abram built an altar and invoked the name of the Lord, he prefigured the Church's Eucharistic sacrifice, where Christ Himself is both priest and victim.

Origen, Homilies on Genesis

The Descent into Egypt

Abram's sojourn in Egypt during the famine is rich in typological significance. Egypt represents the world, the realm of spiritual bondage. Just as Abram went down into Egypt because of famine and later came out enriched, so the Christian must sometimes pass through worldly trials but emerges strengthened by God's providence.

More profoundly, Abram's journey to Egypt and exodus prefigures both the Israelite sojourn under Joseph and Moses, and the flight of the Holy Family when Joseph took Mary and the Child Jesus into Egypt to escape Herod. As Egypt received and then released the chosen family, so the world receives Christ but cannot hold Him.

Sarai as Type of the Church

The beautiful Sarai, desired by Pharaoh but protected by God, has been interpreted as a figure of the Church. The Church is the Bride of Christ, beautiful in holiness, desired by the powers of this world who wish to possess her, yet guarded by divine providence. Pharaoh's plagues when he took Sarai prefigure the divine judgments that fall upon those who persecute the Church.

The Two Covenants

St. Irenaeus sees in Abraham the prefiguring of both covenants:

"Abraham was made the chief and the forerunner of our faith, who did also receive the covenant of circumcision, after that justification by faith which had pertained to him, when he was yet in uncircumcision, so that in him both covenants might be prefigured, that he might be the father of all who follow the Word of God."

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book IV

Abraham, justified by faith before circumcision (Gen 15:6), is father of the Gentiles who believe without the Law. Abraham, receiving circumcision as a sign of the covenant, is father of the Jews who believe. In him, both peoples are united, prefiguring the one Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles alike.

Recapitulation in Christ

Irenaeus's theology of recapitulation (anakephalaiosis) illuminates the entire Abrahamic narrative:

"When Jesus became man, as Adam had been a man, he 'summed up in himself all nations dispersed from Adam downwards, and all languages and generations of men, together with Adam himself.'"

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies

Christ recapitulates and perfects what Abraham began. The blessing promised to all nations through Abraham's seed finds its fulfillment in Christ, who gathers into Himself all the scattered children of God. As Irenaeus beautifully expresses it: "The patriarchs and prophets sowed the word concerning Christ, but the Church reaped, that is, received the fruit."
moral:
Moral (Tropological) Interpretation

The Call to Conversion

The moral sense of Genesis 12 speaks directly to the Christian soul. Abram's call to leave his country and kindred is a call to interior conversion—the fundamental turning from sin to God that marks the beginning of the spiritual life. Every Christian must hear this summons: leave behind the old life of sin, the familiar patterns of vice, the inherited disorders of fallen nature.

St. John Chrysostom, in his Homilies on Genesis, presents Abraham as a model for moral reformation. His purpose in examining the patriarchal narratives was "to provide instruction for the moral reformation of the Christians of Antioch." Abraham demonstrates that even before the Law was given, a person could live virtuously "with only simple trust in God."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis

Faith and Obedience

The defining characteristic of Abraham's response is the union of faith and obedience. "So Abram went out as the Lord had commanded him" (Gen 12:4). As the Letter to the Hebrews declares: "By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed by going out to a place which he was to receive for an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing where he was going" (Heb 11:8).

Chrysostom teaches that Abraham's obedience was exemplary in its promptness and completeness:

"Abraham did not cleave to his kindred, but gave it up as unconcernedly as if he were about to leave a foreign land. When told to offer up his son, he offered him up as if he had no son; as if he had divested himself of his nature."

St. John Chrysostom, Homily 24 on Hebrews

The moral lesson is clear: true faith manifests in obedience. Abraham did not argue, delay, or bargain with God. His speedy and submissive response stands as a model for all believers. As one commentator summarizes: "Abraham's obedience was speedy and without delay, submissive and without dispute; for he went out, not knowing where he went, but knowing whom he followed and under whose direction he went."

Detachment from the World

The threefold command to leave country, kindred, and father's house teaches the necessity of detachment. Gregory of Nyssa, in his spiritual writings, presents Abraham as an exemplar of the soul's journey to God:

"Abraham 'went out not knowing whither he went' yet his mind, unimpeded by any object of sense, was never hindered from its journeying in quest of what lies beyond all that is known, soaring above the things which are cognizable by sense, and from the beauty of the objects of contemplation."

St. Gregory of Nyssa

Detachment does not mean hatred of family or possessions, but the proper ordering of loves. God must come first. When any created good—even the most legitimate—takes precedence over God, it becomes an idol. Abraham's willingness to leave everything demonstrates that nothing earthly can compare to the call of God.

The Virtue of Faith

Chrysostom emphasizes that Abraham was justified by faith, not by works of the Law (which did not yet exist):

"The patriarch Abraham himself before receiving circumcision had been declared righteous on the score of faith alone: before circumcision, the text says, 'Abraham believed God, and credit for it brought him to righteousness.'"

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis, Homily 27

Yet this faith was never separate from virtue. As Chrysostom explains elsewhere: "It is faith and virtue in all cases that is conspicuous and gives the real relationship character," and "noble birth after the flesh is of no avail, but we must seek for virtue of soul." The true children of Abraham are those who imitate both his faith and his virtue.

St. John Chrysostom

Courage in Uncertainty

Abraham departed "not knowing where he was going." This requires immense courage—the willingness to trust God even when the future is obscure. The moral application is that Christians must often act in faith without full knowledge of outcomes. Prudence does not require omniscience; it requires fidelity to God's known will, leaving the unknown future in His hands.

The Danger of Fear

The episode in Egypt reveals a moral failure. Fearing for his life, Abraham resorted to deception, instructing Sarai to claim she was merely his sister. Though the ruse contained a half-truth (she was his half-sister), it was fundamentally dishonest and endangered Sarai's virtue. The Fathers acknowledge this weakness while noting God's faithfulness despite human failings.

The moral lesson is sobering: even the greatest saints can fall into sin when fear replaces faith. Abraham, who trusted God enough to leave everything, nevertheless feared Pharaoh more than he trusted God's protection. Fear is often the root of sin—fear of loss, fear of suffering, fear of death leads us to compromise our integrity.

Building Altars: The Life of Prayer

Wherever Abraham went, he built altars and invoked the name of the Lord. This pattern teaches the necessity of prayer in the Christian life. As the altar represents worship and communion with God, so the faithful must establish "altars" in their daily lives—set times and places for prayer, habits of turning to God in every circumstance.

The building of altars also signifies sacrifice and self-offering. As one source notes: "The altar teaches us, in type, the importance of daily communion with God on the basis of the precious blood of Christ." Christians are called to present themselves "as a living sacrifice" (Rom 12:1), laying every aspect of life on the altar before God.

Generosity and Hospitality

Abraham's character as displayed throughout Genesis 12-25 is marked by generosity. Though later chapters detail his hospitality more fully (especially Genesis 18), the seeds are present here. He shares his journey with Lot, he deals peaceably with others, he enriches rather than impoverishes those around him. The moral lesson is that faith produces generosity; attachment to God frees us from attachment to possessions.

Perseverance Through Trials

No sooner does Abraham enter the promised land than famine strikes. The life of faith is not exempt from trials. Indeed, those whom God calls often face immediate testing. Abraham's perseverance through famine, danger, and uncertainty models the Christian virtue of patient endurance. The promised land was not immediately a land of ease; it became so only through faithful persistence.
anagogical:
Anagogical Interpretation

The Heavenly Country

The anagogical sense of Scripture interprets earthly realities as signs of heavenly glory. Abraham's journey from Ur to the promised land is ultimately a figure of the soul's pilgrimage to heaven. The land of Canaan, though a real earthly inheritance, points beyond itself to the eternal homeland that awaits the faithful.

The Letter to the Hebrews makes this eschatological meaning explicit:

"By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed by going out to a place which he was to receive for an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing where he was going. By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise: For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God."

Hebrews 11:8-10

Abraham lived in tents throughout his life precisely because his eyes were fixed not on any earthly city but on the heavenly Jerusalem. As Hebrews 11:16 continues: "But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city."

The Pilgrim Church

St. Augustine, in his City of God, develops the image of the Church as a pilgrim people journeying through the world toward their eternal homeland:

"The divine oracle to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and all the other prophetic signs given in sacred writings, pertain partly to the nation of Abraham's flesh, and partly to that seed of his in which all nations are blessed as fellow-heirs of Christ by the New Testament. Therefore they pertain partly to the bond maid who genders to bondage—the earthly Jerusalem—but partly to the free city of God, the true Jerusalem eternal in the heavens, whose children are all those that live according to God in the earth."

St. Augustine, City of God

Christians are citizens of heaven living temporarily in the earthly city. Like Abraham, they dwell in tents—their earthly lives are temporary sojourns. Augustine teaches that "the supreme significance of pilgrimage lies in seeking the heavenly Jerusalem, the eternal reality of which the earthly city is but a shadow."

The Two Cities

Augustine's great theme of the two cities—the City of God and the City of Man—finds its origin in the Abrahamic narrative. From the line of Seth descends Noah, from Noah his sons, and from Shem comes Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and ultimately Christ. This lineage constitutes the City of God journeying through history.

"The two peoples are fundamentally distinguished by their two kinds of loves: the earthly city was created by self-love reaching the point of contempt for God, the Heavenly City by the love of God carried as far as contempt of self."

St. Augustine, City of God

Abraham's departure from Ur represents the separation of the City of God from the City of Man. His refusal to settle permanently in Canaan, his life in tents, his building of altars—all signify the pilgrim character of God's people who seek a homeland not made with hands.

The Blessing of All Nations: The Eschatological Gathering

The promise that "in thee shall all the kindred of the earth be blessed" finds its ultimate fulfillment in the eschatological gathering of the nations. The Book of Revelation depicts this vision: "After this I saw a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne, and in sight of the Lamb" (Rev 7:9).

The seed of Abraham, which is Christ, will gather to Himself a people from every nation under heaven. This gathering, begun in the Church's mission, will be consummated at the end of time when Christ returns in glory. The blessing promised to Abraham thus extends to the eschaton—the final state of blessedness for all who believe.

Present Hope and Future Glory

St. John Chrysostom, commenting on Hebrews, connects the promises to Abraham with Christian hope:

"If these came to pass after so long a time, so certainly the others will. So that the things which happened in regard to Abraham give us confidence also concerning the things to come... While we are still in the world, and not yet departed from this life, we are already among the promises. For through hope we are already in heaven."

St. John Chrysostom, Homily on Hebrews

The Christian lives in the tension between "already" and "not yet." Through faith and baptism, believers already participate in the promises made to Abraham. Yet the fullness of those promises awaits the resurrection of the body and the life of the world to come. Abraham's patient waiting for the promised land models the Christian's patient waiting for the heavenly country.

The Resurrection and the Land

The land promised to Abraham's seed is ultimately the new heavens and new earth promised in Isaiah and Revelation. The resurrection of the body ensures that the inheritance is not merely spiritual but includes a renewed material creation. Abraham's seed will inherit not just Canaan, not just the spiritual blessings of the Church, but the entire cosmos restored and glorified.

As Augustine explains, the pilgrimage of the City of God through history arrives at its destination "in union with God at the eschaton." The telos—the final end—of Abraham's journey is nothing less than the beatific vision, the perfect enjoyment of God in the communion of saints.

Egypt and the World

Abraham's descent into Egypt and subsequent exodus prefigures the Christian's passage through the world. Egypt represents the realm of bondage, the dominion of sin and death. But just as Abraham passed through Egypt and emerged enriched, so the Christian passes through this world of trials and emerges into eternal glory, bearing the treasures of grace accumulated along the way.

The plagues that fell upon Pharaoh when he took Sarai also prefigure the final judgment. Those who persecute the Church, who seek to possess what belongs to God alone, will face divine retribution. The vindication of Abraham and Sarai is a type of the final vindication of all the faithful when Christ returns to judge the living and the dead.

The Eternal Altar

The altars Abraham built in Canaan find their ultimate fulfillment in the heavenly liturgy. In the Book of Revelation, the altar before God's throne is the site of perpetual worship: "And another angel came, and stood before the altar, having a golden censer" (Rev 8:3). The earthly altars of Abraham, the Temple altar in Jerusalem, and the Christian altar where the Eucharist is celebrated are all anticipations of this eternal worship.

In heaven, the people of God gathered from every nation will offer unending praise to the God who called Abraham and fulfilled all His promises. The communion begun in faith will be perfected in sight. As St. Basil prayed: "May the Father of the true light, Who reserves for us in the peace of a future age a spiritual and everlasting light, enlighten your hearts in the knowledge of truth... Thus shall you shine as the sun in the midst of the glory of the saints."

St. Basil the Great, Hexaemeron

The Wedding Feast

Finally, the union of Abraham and Sarah prefigures the eternal union of Christ and His Bride, the Church. The marriage of the Lamb, celebrated in the heavenly Jerusalem, fulfills all that was begun in the patriarchal narratives. Abraham, who received the promise that all nations would be blessed through him, will see that promise fulfilled when the great multitude stands before the throne, clothed in white robes, celebrating the wedding feast that has no end.
